phy-gi-201.why: Metabolism covers the body's chemical reactions. Anabolic pathways build larger molecules, whereas catabolic pathways break down molecules and can release usable energy.

notes.A: This is the overall definition of metabolism and includes pathways in every tissue.
notes.B: Building complex molecules from smaller precursors is anabolism, one part of metabolism.
notes.C: Breaking complex molecules into smaller products is catabolism, the other broad part of metabolism.
notes.D: Both anabolic and catabolic pathways are included, often with intermediates linking the two.

phy-gi-204.why: Intestinal absorption transfers digested material across the mucosa. At the brush border, SGLT1 uses the sodium gradient to take glucose into an enterocyte. Glucose then leaves across the basolateral membrane and reaches villus capillaries.

notes.A: Peristalsis moves material along the lumen. This is propulsion and involves no transfer across the epithelium.
notes.C: Peptide hydrolysis is chemical digestion. It supplies amino acids that can subsequently be absorbed.
notes.D: Duodenal acid stimulates S cells to release secretin. This is endocrine signalling in response to luminal contents.
notes.E: Peptide hydrolysis is digestion, while secretin release is endocrine secretion. Both can precede absorption.

phy-gi-205.why: Chewing physically fragments food. The smaller pieces have more exposed surface area for digestive enzymes, and mixing with saliva moistens the bolus for swallowing.

notes.A: Fat and amino acids in the duodenum stimulate CCK release, which contracts the gallbladder. Chewing aids digestion directly by fragmenting food.
notes.C: Hydrolysis of peptide bonds requires proteases such as pepsin, which acts in the stomach.
notes.D: Salivary amylase hydrolyses starch while the food is being chewed. That chemical reaction is due to the enzyme.
notes.E: Lingual and gastric lipases can hydrolyse some triglyceride. The teeth break up food particles without hydrolysing lipid molecules.

phy-gi-206.why: The small intestine is the main site of nutrient uptake. Villi and brush-border microvilli enlarge the absorptive surface. Most water-soluble nutrients enter villus capillaries, while chylomicrons first enter the lacteals.

notes.A: Hepatocytes produce bile. The small intestine receives bile through the bile duct and uses its bile salts during lipid digestion.
notes.B: Blood filtration and removal of many soluble wastes are functions of the kidneys.
notes.C: Some vitamins are made by intestinal bacteria, especially in the colon. The small-intestinal epithelium is specialised for nutrient uptake.
notes.E: Hydrochloric acid is secreted by gastric parietal cells. Bicarbonate helps neutralise that acid when chyme reaches the duodenum.

phy-gi-225.why: The mucosa lines the gut lumen. Its epithelium contains absorptive cells and secretory cells, and its glands contribute secretions suited to each segment of the tract.

notes.B: The submucosa contains vessels, lymphatics and a nerve plexus. Some regions have submucosal glands, but the surface epithelium performs most absorption.
notes.C: The muscularis externa contains smooth muscle layers that mix and propel the contents.
notes.D: The serosa is an outer mesothelial covering that reduces friction where the gut is covered by peritoneum.
notes.E: The adventitia is external connective tissue that anchors parts of the gut to surrounding structures.

phy-gi-228.why: The small intestine is the principal site of digestion overall. Segmentation mixes chyme with bile and pancreatic juice, and pancreatic and brush-border enzymes complete most chemical digestion. The stomach also provides substantial mechanical mixing.

notes.A: The pylorus regulates the passage of chyme into the duodenum. Antral grinding helps reduce particle size before emptying.
notes.B: The gastric fundus is a reservoir that accommodates a meal. Much of the vigorous gastric grinding takes place farther distally.
notes.C: The stomach churns food and starts substantial protein digestion, but most enzymatic breakdown of the meal is completed downstream.
notes.D: The large intestine absorbs water and electrolytes and supports bacterial fermentation of residual substrates. It receives chyme after most digestion has occurred.

phy-gi-233.why: Specialised enteroendocrine cells release hormones across the basolateral membrane. Circulating hormones such as gastrin and cholecystokinin alter digestive secretion or motility at their target tissues.

notes.A: Exocrine glands release products into the lumen via ducts or epithelial surfaces. Endocrine release delivers a signal to the circulation.
notes.C: The stomach produces hormones such as gastrin, but its immediate protection from acid and pepsin depends heavily on the mucus and bicarbonate barrier.
notes.D: Enterocytes are chiefly absorptive cells. Specialised enteroendocrine cells provide the principal endocrine signals from the gut epithelium.
notes.E: Mucosal protection depends on epithelial barriers and protective secretions. Digestive hormones act as regulatory signals from multiple gut regions.

phy-gi-300.why: Erythropoietin is produced mainly by renal interstitial cells in adults in response to hypoxia. It stimulates red cell production in bone marrow. The other options are signalling peptides produced in the gut.

notes.A: Cholecystokinin is secreted by small-intestinal I cells and promotes gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion.
notes.B: Gastrin is released from G cells, chiefly in the gastric antrum, and stimulates acid secretion.
notes.C: Secretin comes from duodenal S cells in response to acid and increases bicarbonate secretion by the pancreas.
notes.E: Somatostatin from gastric and intestinal D cells acts locally and can inhibit gastrin and other digestive secretions.

phy-gi-203.why: Salivary glands secrete alpha-amylase into the mouth, and pancreatic acinar cells secrete it into pancreatic juice. Both enzymes hydrolyse internal alpha-1,4 linkages in starch.

notes.A: The liver produces bile, and the duodenum receives pancreatic amylase. Neither is a major source of digestive alpha-amylase.
notes.B: Pancreatic acini produce amylase. The duodenum is the site where that enzyme is delivered and acts.
notes.C: Salivary glands produce amylase, but the liver contributes bile rather than the second major supply of digestive amylase.
notes.E: The stomach secretes pepsinogen, and the duodenum receives amylase from the pancreas. Salivary amylase can act briefly after swallowing.

phy-gi-226.why: Alpha-amylase is secreted into saliva and pancreatic juice. It hydrolyses starch to smaller carbohydrates, which brush-border enzymes then convert to absorbable monosaccharides.

notes.A: Maltase activity is present in the intestinal brush border and releases glucose from maltose.
notes.C: Chief cells in the stomach secrete pepsinogen, which becomes pepsin in the acidic gastric lumen.
notes.D: Pancreatic nucleases are delivered to the small intestine to digest nucleic acids. They are not the digestive enzyme shared with saliva.
notes.E: The pancreas secretes trypsinogen, which is activated in the small intestine. Salivary glands do not supply digestive trypsinogen.

phy-gi-261.why: The salivary glands can concentrate inorganic iodide from plasma through sodium–iodide symporter activity. Salivary iodide can exceed twice the plasma concentration, although the ratio varies with iodine exposure and flow.

notes.A: Parotid saliva is predominantly serous, while sublingual secretion is relatively rich in mucins. Composition also varies with stimulation.
notes.B: Salivary amylase starts starch digestion. The main digestive proteases act in the stomach and small intestine.
notes.C: Salivary ionised calcium varies with the sample and flow conditions. A fixed ratio below half the plasma value is an unreliable general description.
notes.E: Salivary pH depends on flow and bicarbonate. Stimulated saliva is often near neutral or slightly alkaline.

phy-gi-262.why: The oral phase of swallowing begins voluntarily as the tongue moves the bolus posteriorly. The medullary swallowing pattern then coordinates pharyngeal propulsion, airway closure and a brief pause in breathing.

notes.A: The central swallowing pattern is coordinated in the brainstem, with key control circuits in the medulla.
notes.C: The thoracic spinal cord is not the swallowing centre. Vagal and enteric circuits coordinate oesophageal passage after the pharyngeal phase.
notes.D: The distal smooth-muscle oesophagus has intrinsic neural circuits that help coordinate its peristaltic contractions.
notes.E: Oesophageal peristalsis moves a bolus in either position. When upright, gravity can assist rather than impede passage.

phy-gi-298.why: Resting lower oesophageal sphincter pressure adds to the antireflux barrier at the gastro-oesophageal junction. The sphincter relaxes during swallowing and usually regains tone after the bolus passes.

notes.A: The lower oesophageal sphincter has a sustained resting pressure above that of the adjacent oesophageal body.
notes.C: The antireflux barrier can weaken in pregnancy, with reduced resting pressure or a diminished sphincter response.
notes.D: Pharmacological gastrin can raise sphincter pressure. The normal response varies, so a simple fall in tone is not expected.
notes.E: Cholinergic input supports sphincter contraction. Antimuscarinic drugs can reduce basal pressure rather than reinforce the barrier.

phy-gi-312.why: Saliva starts starch digestion, lubricates the bolus and helps protect the mouth. Complete digestion of protein requires proteases and peptidases acting in the stomach and small intestine.

notes.A: Water and mucins lubricate food and help form a cohesive bolus that can be swallowed.
notes.B: Saliva buffers plaque acids and supplies calcium and phosphate for enamel remineralisation. Both actions help protect against dental caries.
notes.D: Salivary gland cells can concentrate iodide from plasma. Iodide in saliva can contribute to local antimicrobial chemistry.
notes.E: Bicarbonate and other salivary buffers limit oral pH swings, although the pH is not fixed at exactly seven.

phy-gi-208.why: Gastric parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid, so gastric juice has the lowest pH among these secretions. Duodenal bicarbonate then helps neutralise the acidic chyme.

notes.B: Hepatic bile is relatively alkaline and contains bile salts that assist in processing dietary lipids.
notes.C: Pancreatic duct cells secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid, which raises the pH of acidic duodenal contents.
notes.D: Saliva typically has a near-neutral pH, with higher bicarbonate concentrations at higher flow.
notes.E: Intestinal secretions are generally near neutral to alkaline. Duodenal mucus and bicarbonate help protect the surface from gastric acid.

phy-gi-210.why: Parietal cells release hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor into the gastric lumen. During acid secretion, bicarbonate enters the blood through the basolateral chloride–bicarbonate exchanger, contributing to the postprandial alkaline tide.

notes.B: Hydrochloric acid comes from parietal cells. Pepsinogen is released into gastric glands by chief cells.
notes.C: Hydrogen ions are released into the gastric lumen. Bicarbonate moves to the blood, so it is not part of the parietal cell's luminal output.
notes.D: Intrinsic factor is released into the lumen. Bicarbonate exits at the basolateral side, while hydrochloric acid is the other key luminal product.
notes.E: Mucous epithelial cells secrete mucus, and chief cells release pepsinogen. Neither is the characteristic luminal secretion of parietal cells.

phy-gi-211.why: Gastric acid produces a low pH that initiates cleavage of inactive pepsinogen to active pepsin. Pepsin then activates further pepsinogen and cleaves dietary proteins in the acidic gastric lumen.

notes.A: Pancreatic lipase acts in the less acidic environment of the small intestine, where bicarbonate neutralises gastric acid.
notes.B: Lingual lipase is secreted as an enzyme that can work in acidic gastric contents. Pepsinogen, by comparison, requires cleavage of an inactive precursor.
notes.C: Intrinsic factor is a binding protein for vitamin B12. Gastric acid helps release dietary B12 from food proteins, rather than activating intrinsic factor.
notes.E: Bile salts form mixed micelles with lipid digestion products in the small intestine. Gastric acid is not the mechanism for this step.

phy-gi-218.why: Vagal input normally promotes acid secretion through direct cholinergic effects and indirect stimulation of gastrin and histamine pathways. Inhibiting this input decreases its stimulatory effect on parietal cells.

notes.B: Peptides and amino acids stimulate gastrin release, which can increase acid secretion during the gastric phase.
notes.C: Histamine activates parietal H2 receptors, increasing cAMP and stimulating the gastric proton pump.
notes.D: Acetylcholine stimulates muscarinic receptors on parietal cells and increases acid secretion.
notes.E: Gastric distension activates local and vagovagal reflexes that promote acid secretion during a meal.

phy-gi-227.why: The pyloric sphincter controls gastric emptying. Antral contractions drive larger particles back for further grinding when the outlet narrows, while small volumes of suitably processed chyme pass into the duodenum.

notes.A: The oesophageal sphincters regulate entry into the oesophagus or stomach. They do not meter gastric emptying into the intestine.
notes.B: An intrinsic sphincter is a general description and does not specify the muscular ring at the gastric outlet.
notes.C: The cardiac sphincter is the lower oesophageal sphincter at the entrance to the stomach. It helps prevent reflux.
notes.E: The sphincter between the stomach and proximal duodenum is anatomically the pyloric sphincter.

phy-gi-229.why: Parietal cells use an apical hydrogen–potassium ATPase to secrete hydrogen ions into the gastric lumen. Chloride enters the lumen separately, yielding hydrochloric acid. These cells also secrete intrinsic factor.

notes.A: Serotonin is characteristic of enterochromaffin cells. Gastric enterochromaffin-like cells instead release histamine near parietal cells.
notes.B: Surface and neck mucous cells provide gastric mucus. Surface mucus and bicarbonate protect the lining from acid.
notes.C: Pepsinogen is released chiefly by gastric chief cells and becomes active after exposure to gastric acid.
notes.E: G cells, chiefly in the antrum, secrete gastrin and thereby stimulate acid production downstream.
